I'll define near-duplicates that way (integer columns equal, bmi within 0.1, pedigree within 0.005), then count clusters and check outcome consistency.

input.command:
cd /home/daytona/workspace && python3 -c "
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
from scipy.sparse.csgraph import connected_components
from scipy.sparse import csr_matrix
df=pd.read_csv('data.csv')
ints=['pregnancies','glucose','blood_pressure','skin_thickness','insulin','age']
for bt,pt in [(0.1,0.005),(0.1,0.01),(0.2,0.01),(0.05,0.005)]:
    n=len(df); A=np.zeros((n,n),bool)
    for c,g in df.groupby(ints).groups.items():
        g=np.array(list(g))
        if len(g)<2: continue
        b=df.loc[g,'bmi'].values; p=df.loc[g,'diabetes_pedigree'].values
        m=(np.abs(b[:,None]-b[None,:])<=bt+1e-9)&(np.abs(p[:,None]-p[None,:])<=pt+1e-9)
        A[np.ix_(g,g)]=m
    nc,lab=connected_components(csr_matrix(A),directed=False)
    d=df.assign(cl=lab)
    conf=(d.groupby('cl').outcome.nunique()>1).sum()
    print(bt,pt,'clusters',nc,'removed',n-nc,'conflicting clusters',conf)
"

content.text:
The random forest gets **79.7% accuracy** (0.797) on the held-out test set, with 133 test rows.

The file had 921 rows, more than the 768 in the Pima diabetes dataset it resembles, so I checked for duplicates. There were 57 exact duplicates, plus many altered copies. In those, the integer columns matched exactly and only `bmi` or `diabetes_pedigree` differed by rounding-level amounts (e.g. 27.2 vs 27.262). I removed 260 near-duplicates (identical integer columns, bmi within 0.1, pedigree within 0.005), leaving 661 rows. No duplicate group had conflicting outcomes, so the removal didn't merge different labels. I then made a stratified 80/20 split (`random_state=42`): 528 training rows and 133 test rows. The test score comes from that split made after deduplication.

The model is a `RandomForestClassifier` (500 trees, `random_state=42`) trained on the 8 medical features. Training accuracy is 1.0, so the model overfits somewhat, but the test score is what I report.

Files written to `/home/daytona/workspace`:
- `train.csv` (528 rows) and `test.csv` (133 rows): the cleaned rows used for training and testing, with all columns.
- `report.json`: test accuracy, model description, and a note on the deduplication.
- `predictions.csv`: one `prediction` column with 154 rows, in the same order as `holdout_features.csv`. The predictions come from the model trained on the training set only.

I didn't create any charts, so `live/` is empty.
